newsitem.title: GERMANY: Waigel rejects calls for exchange rate moves.
newsitem.headline: Waigel rejects calls for exchange rate moves.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Friday rejected criticism of the monetary policies of Bundesbank and said economic growth and jobs could not be achieved through targeted exchange rate policies.

Waigel's statements come a day after a member of the Bank of France council attacked the Bundesbank, saying devalution of the French franc against the mark could be necessary because of German incomprehension on monetary and exchange rate policy.
Waigel said those in Europe who considered a stability pact for European economic and monetary union less important than a pact for jobs were "embarking on a dangerous path".

"A European stability pact ensures the stability of the euro. Only a stable monetary union can create economic growth and jobs in Germany and Europe," he said. "Growth and jobs cannot be created through targeted exchange policies."

Bank of France member Jean-Pierre Gerard said on Thursday devaluation of the French currency against the mark was undesirable but possibly necessary because of German incomprehension on monetary and exchange rate policy.

Gerard also said that Italy should be in on the creation of a euro single currency and bluntly accused Germany of resisting a country which had founded the European Union with France and Germany and which should be with them in launching the euro.

Gerard, a member of the independent central bank's monetary policy council and believed to be one of a minority in favour of less stringent monetary policy within the Bank's inner sanctum, laid out his views in a newspaper interview.
Germany has taken a hard line on observance of the fiscal criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) as set out in the Maastricth Treaty.

It is seeking a stablity pact with sanctions against EMU participants who make the grade for entry into EMU in 1999 but then ease fiscal discipline and allow budget deficits and public debt to exceed the Maastricht targets.
"Whoever thinks a European stability pact is less important than a pact for jobs is embarking on a dangerous path," Waigel said.
